title: llm-prefetch-kv-cache-scratchpad
body:
Purpose:
- quick personal brain dump/parking lot for ideas around prefetching / KV-cache warm strategies for the serving runtime. rough PRD-ish notes, user stories, experiments, and open questions.

Context / motivation:
- latency-sensitive apps suffer from cold KV cache for long-form generation (esp. multi-turn chat with long contexts).
- current approach: warm on first request, rely on batching to amortize tokens. but single-user low qps patterns (single-head chat apps) see high p99 token latencies and higher token cost because batch sizes are small.
- goal: reduce first-token latency and p95/p99 of token generation for long-context dialogs without increasing cost materially.

Idea summary (high level):
1) Predictive prefetching: based on routing + user/session signals, proactively load KV cache for the most-likely next model variant + sequence prefixes.
2) Background async warmers: keep a small per-customer warm pool (configured) that maintains KV caches for popular prompts/roles.
3) Hierarchical cache: fast RAM LRU per-GPU + shared cold pool across pods (on-NVMe) + network fast-transfer for quick reload.
4) Tiny compressed checkpoints: store quantized KV checkpoints for common prefixes to speed restore.

User stories / acceptance criteria (draft):
- As a product engineer building a chat app, I want first-token latency for new sessions to be < 150ms for short prompts and < 400ms for long-context prompts, 90% of the time.
- As infra owner, I want warmers to not increase per-token cost by more than 5% on average across a workload mix.
- As platform operator, I want controls to set per-customer warm pool size and eviction policy (default safe limits).

Proposed experiments / signals to collect:
- Baseline metrics: per-request first-token latency distribution by session age (new vs returning), sequence-length, model, region.
- Experiment: enable predictive prefetch for a subset of tenants. Measure p50/p95/p99 first-token latency, cost per token, GPU utilization, and additional network egress.
- Key signals: prefix-hit-rate (how often prefetch matched actual next prefix), wasted-prefetch-rate (prefetches not used within TTL), average restore-time-from-checkpoint, warm-pool-memory-usage.

Prefetch heuristics (brainstorm):
- session-based: if session has seen a template prompt (e.g., "Summarize: ..."), prefetch likely continuation variants.
- user-behavior signals: rising probability of long generation after certain triggers (file-upload, tool-call).
- routing + model-variant mapping: if policy routes a request to xlarge-8q, prefetch the matching quantized checkpoint.
- time-windowed frequency: keep top-k prefixes for last N minutes per-customer.

Implementation sketch (runtime interactions) - high level:
- on request arrival, compute warm-key: (customer, model_id, prefix-hash, device-class). check local L1 KV cache.
- if miss, check shared L2 (fast NVMe pool). if present, async restore to L1 and start streaming generation (optimistically run without full KV for first chunk if possible).
- background prefetch worker: consumes hot-prefix table, does checkpoint restore into L2 or L1 depending on policy.

Pseudocode notes: (very rough)
- hot_prefixes = sliding-window top-k per-customer
- prefetch_worker: for prefix in hot_prefixes: if not in L2 or L1: restore_checkpoint(prefix)
- on_request(req): key = hash(req.prefix); if key in L1: use; elif key in L2: schedule async copy to L1 and proceed; else: on-demand create (longer tail)

Risks / open questions:
- increased memory pressure on GPUs leading to reduced concurrency. need forecasts and safe defaults.
- fairness across tenants: warm pool must be quota-limited. prioritize paying tiers? policy decision.
- security: KV caches contain token-level state, sensitive context may be cached. ensure per-tenant isolation and encryption at rest for L2.
- correctness: restoring KV mid-generation must preserve deterministic outputs; potential for subtle divergence if misaligned. need tests.

Operational controls and UX:
- console controls: per-tenant warm pool size, prefetch aggressiveness slider (off / conservative / aggressive), TTLs.
- telemetry: dashboard showing prefetch hit/miss, wasted-prefetch-rate, memory usage, p99 latency delta vs baseline.
- automated fallback: when memory pressure high, reduce prefetch or evict LRU across low-tier tenants.

Experiment cadence / milestones (rough):
- week 0-2: instrument metrics (prefix frequency, restore-time), collect baselines across representative tenants.
- week 3-6: implement L2 checkpoint restore prototype + simulate prefetch logic in canary. run offline replay to estimate hit rates.
- week 7-10: small canary with 5% traffic for 2 small tenants; measure latency and cost. iterate heuristics.
- week 11-14: widen to more tenants and test policy controls.

Sensible defaults / guardrails:
- default warm-pool-memory per-customer: small (e.g., 200MB) unless requested.
- prefetch TTL: 30s by default.
- per-customer max prefetch ops/sec: 1-2/sec to avoid overload.

Open TODOs (personal):
- talk to SRE (Miguel) about L2 storage options + perf for restore (NVMe vs memcached).
- ask security (Priya) about allowed retention of KV snapshots and encryption requirements.
- sketch UI mock for warm pool controls in console (measure permissions model).
- run offline replay on last-30-days to get prefix top-k and potential hit rate estimate (ask infra for sample trace).

Notes to self:
- prioritize experiments that don't require kernel/LLM changes (use restore + copy path) to get early signal.
- keep the first canary on small models (7B) to avoid cost surprises.

Links / references (internal):
- earlier notes: users/llm-caching-scratchpad (compare)
- git PR for checkpoint-restore: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/486
- related jira: JIRA-INV-7890 (prefetch infra spike)

Random brain dump / fringe ideas:
- collaborate with Optimize: suggest per-workload quantization variants that optimize checkpoint sizes for faster restore.
- memory-lite kv: store only attention keys for recent N tokens (instead of full kv) to reduce checkpoint size for warmers.
- predictive batching: if prefetch worker can predict multiple upcoming prefixes, warm them and then attempt to form synthetic batches for low-qps flows (risky).

End of scratchpad.
summary: Personal scratchpad: prefetching and KV-cache warm strategy brainstorm. includes user stories, experiments, heuristics, risks, and TODOs.
